abstract: |
  Creative products are assessed by consensus of independent raters. How many raters are needed and how raters differ have been studied mostly with verbal and static material; such evidence is lacking for nonverbal, time-pressured products such as football actions. Twenty-five raters gave 9,831 ratings of 3,841 actions on a 7-point creativity scale in an incomplete, connected design. We fitted a graded response model (GRM) and nested models from the rating-scale many-facet Rasch model to the generalized partial credit model, and examined reliability by number of ratings, observed and simulated. The empirical reliability of the obtained scores was .695, against .970 for a hypothetical full panel; single ratings agreed at Krippendorff's α = .402, while Cronbach's α (18 raters) was .959. Mean product-level reliability was .526 with one rating and .703 with two; the smallest number of ratings at which simulated reliability reached .80 was four. Raters differed in severity (2.388 logits), category use, thresholds, discrimination and information; parameters were imprecise for some raters, not only those with about 50 ratings. Likelihood-ratio tests rejected a shared category structure and equal discrimination (both *p* < .001), whereas the Bayesian information criterion favoured the constrained models in both cases. With one rating, raw means and GRM scores agreed at Kendall's τ-b = .773 (.076 of pairs in reversed order). Studies of such products should report the reliability of the scores actually used, plan several ratings per action from domain-specific evidence, link raters through a common calibration set, and consider rater-adjusting scoring models.

# Introduction

Creativity is widely regarded as a core competence. Employers rank creative thinking among the core skills of the workforce [@wef2025], the Programme for International Student Assessment assessed creative thinking in its 2022 cycle [@oecd2024], and in sport, creativity is considered a quality to be developed and evaluated in players [@safardilha2019; @santos2016]. By the standard definition, a creative product is both original and effective [@stein1953; @runco2012]. How creativity should be assessed is less settled: enduring conceptual and methodological issues and the lack of established assessment standards continue to limit creativity research [@barbot2019]. The design of a creativity assessment therefore has to be justified by evidence. [\[FILL IN: verify the framing claims attributed to wef2025, oecd2024, safardilha2019 and santos2016, the definition attributed to stein1953, and the barbot2019 statement (p. 131) against the PDFs (FI-17)\]]{.mark}

Creativity research distinguishes four facets, the person, the process, the press and the product [@rhodes1961]. In the framework of @batey2012, the present study is located at the level of the individual, at the product facet and at ratings by others, and each facet requires its own measurement approach [@barbot2019b]. [\[FILL IN: verify the four facets in rhodes1961 and the wording of the three framework cells in batey2012 (FI-17)\]]{.mark} Creative products are assessed by the consensus of independent raters who know the domain: the consensual assessment technique [CAT; @amabile1982; @hennessey2011; @kaufman2024]. In the CAT and judge response theory literature, raters are called judges; we use "raters" throughout. The consensus, however, is only as good as the panel that produces it.

## How many raters are enough is conditional

The reliability of CAT scores rests on aggregation. As @amabile1982 noted, by Spearman–Brown logic the reliability of a mean rating depends on the mean inter-rater correlation and on the number of raters, so that a larger panel compensates for lower agreement between individual raters. The reverse also holds: coefficient alpha rises with the size of the panel alone, so a high alpha from a large panel says little about the agreement between single raters. Nor does a high alpha ensure that a panel converges with experts: @kaufman2008a reported that 106 novices reached an alpha of .94 on poems while correlating .22 with experts. [\[FILL IN: verify the values .94 and .22 in kaufman2008a and that .22 is the correlation of the novice panel with the expert panel (FI-17)\]]{.mark} Moreover, consistency and absolute agreement are seldom distinguished in creativity research [@cseh2019; @stefanic2015].

How many raters are needed therefore depends on the reliability target, on the object of measurement (persons across tasks or single products), on rater expertise and training, on the scale and scoring format, on the heterogeneity of the products and on the domain. The published evidence bears this out, and each figure has to be read with its target and object. One body of evidence concerns persons who are measured across tasks. For short divergent-thinking responses, D-studies projected that two trained student raters for unusual uses and instances and three for consequences would reach a relative generalizability coefficient of at least .80 under average scoring [@silvia2008]. For captions, a creative-writing task, five graduate-student raters with 15 captions were projected to reach .80 for both relative and absolute coefficients [@kaufman2007]. Where the person-by-task variance is large, adding raters stops helping: with two divergent-thinking items, no panel of one to 10 lay raters reached .80, and rater main effects, which indicate severity differences, accounted for 26.6% and 56.9% of the variance [@hass2018]; with two trained raters, five tasks were needed for a relative coefficient of .70 for originality and completeness (three for practicality), and absolute decisions required more tasks, more raters or both [@vanhooijdonk2022]; and dependability was low for all rater groups on science tasks [@long2015]. [\[FILL IN: verify the figures and verification levels of silvia2008, kaufman2007, hass2018, vanhooijdonk2022 and long2015 as used here (FI-17)\]]{.mark}

A second body of evidence concerns single products. For novices rating expert-domain products with Cronbach's alpha as the criterion, the picture is different: for poems, Kaufman et al.'s own Spearman–Brown projection to 10 novices gave .58 [@kaufman2008a]; for short stories, 100 random panels of 10 novices averaged .53 (range .35–.75) and for five engineering designs .66, against .93 for 10 expert writers and .86 for 15 professional engineers, and 10-novice panels correlated .56 with experts on stories [@kaufman2013]. For open-ended products rated by non-experts, seven or more raters were needed for fashion outfits to exceed inter-rater and test-retest intraclass correlations of .70 consistently [@barth2021], and 10–15 undergraduates for creativity ratings of design products against a test-retest intraclass correlation of .70, with 15–20 for composite indices [@terai2026]. [\[FILL IN: verify the figures and verification levels of kaufman2008a, kaufman2013 (including the expert panels: .93 for 10 expert writers, .86 for 15 professional engineers), barth2021 and terai2026 as used here (FI-17)\]]{.mark}

Practice does not follow these figures closely. Most of 84 reviewed studies used fewer than 10 raters, about five on average [@long2022]; the common recommendation is five to 10 [@kaufman2008], and reported panels run from two to 134 raters [@cseh2019]. We located no study of the required number of raters for sport, for music (as a number of raters), for mathematics, for advertising or for programming. [\[FILL IN: verify long2022, kaufman2008 and cseh2019 as used here (FI-17)\]]{.mark} No general required number exists, then; the published figures are conditional on target, object, raters, scale and domain. @cseh2019 list the number of raters needed for a reliable consensus among the open questions of the CAT, and authors working with generalizability theory argue that each assessment procedure needs its own G- and D-study [@vanhooijdonk2022]. The evidence that does exist, moreover, comes from a narrow range of material.

## The verbal bias and the sport case

The rating-design evidence comes largely from verbal material, that is divergent-thinking responses, poems, stories, captions and metaphors, and from static products that raters inspect at leisure, such as collages, drawings and designs [@amabile1982; @kaufman2008a; @reiterpalmon2019; @saidmetwaly2017b; @paca2019; @acar2023; @acar2024]. Within sport, the standard tests are tests of generalist thinking expressed verbally or through drawing [@safardilha2019]. [\[FILL IN: check the wording and page of the safardilha2019 quotation and the characterisation of reiterpalmon2019, saidmetwaly2017b and paca2019 (FI-17)\]]{.mark}

Football actions are a different kind of product. They are nonverbal behaviour produced under time pressure in a complex, dynamic environment: creative motor actions emerge from the interaction of performer and environment [@orth2017; @hristovski2011; @hristovski2012; @vaughan2019; @rasmussen2019], decisions in team sport are time-constrained option generation [@raab2007], and players have to process substantial information within a very short time [@memmert2011b]. Observed in competition, the product class has been argued to be more ecologically valid than laboratory and game-test settings [@safardilha2019; @memmert2011b; @joode2023; @cotter2019], and ratings of such actions exist [@kempe2018; @joode2023; @zahno2023; @zahno2024]. [\[FILL IN: verify the characterisation of orth2017, hristovski2011, hristovski2012 (author field), vaughan2019, rasmussen2019, raab2007, memmert2011b and cotter2019 (author field Cotter & Silvia) (FI-17)\]]{.mark}

Sport creativity research, however, has concentrated on process measures, divergent thinking in game situations in particular [@memmert2007; @memmert2010; @memmert2013; @furley2015; @roca2018; @fink2018; @safardilha2019; @memmert2011b]. The few studies that had experts rate creative behaviour in football, in competition footage [@kempe2018], in games of academy players [@joode2023], in game-test situations [@memmert2010] or in verbal responses to video scenes [@roca2018], relied on three or four coaches or trained experts and reported the agreement of the panel, as an intraclass correlation in three of them [@memmert2010; @roca2018; @joode2023]. None examined how many raters are needed, how individual raters differ, or which scoring model suits the ratings. [\[FILL IN: verify kempe2018 (scale 0–10 or 1–10, reliability index, training, coaching licence), roca2018, memmert2010 and joode2023 (three or four raters, expertise, ICC, averaging), and the panel sizes of zahno2023 and zahno2024 (FI-17)\]]{.mark} Rating-design evidence for this product class is thus lacking, and answering these questions requires a method that treats the raters themselves as the object of study.

## From averages to judge response theory

Raw averages with alpha or Spearman–Brown treat raters as interchangeable and conflate panel size with agreement. Alpha ignores severity, which confounds raw means whenever different raters rate different products [@primi2019; @myszkowski2019]. Resampling raters from a large pool [@kaufman2013; @barth2021; @terai2026] shows how reliability is distributed across panels of a given size, but its results are specific to that pool. Generalizability theory with D-studies [@silvia2008; @hass2018; @vanhooijdonk2022] decomposes the variance into rater, product and interaction components and projects relative and absolute coefficients to any number of raters, but it still treats raters as interchangeable, needs near-balanced designs and cannot correct individual raters. Classical scoring remains the default in creativity measurement, and item response theory or generalizability theory are rarely used [@saidmetwaly2017b].

Many-facet Rasch models (MFRM) add rater severity as a facet, estimate and correct it in incomplete but connected designs, and flag misfitting raters [@linacre1989; @eckes2015]. @primi2019 showed that severity confounds scores when raters score different subsets of the products and that rater workload could be cut by about a third with severity-adjusted scores. Every Rasch-family model, however, assumes that all raters discriminate equally, and the rating-scale form assumes in addition that all raters share one category structure; differences in discrimination have no parameter and surface only as misfit [@myford2004; @myszkowski2021]. [\[FILL IN: verify primi2019 (workload cut by about a third) and eckes2015 as the source for the partial-credit MFRM (FI-17)\]]{.mark}

Judge response theory (JRT) transposes item response theory to multiple-rater data: raters take the role of items, and their severity, category thresholds and discrimination are estimated individually under the graded response model or the generalized partial credit model. It yields scores with product-specific standard errors, reliability conditional on the creativity level, and an explicit model of rater behaviour in which part of the rater-by-product interaction becomes information rather than error [@myszkowski2019; @myszkowski2021]. It has since been applied to ratings of three-dimensional drawings [@barbot2023], to divergent-thinking ratings, for which a graded response model was retained [@pellegrino2025], to the planning of planned-missing rating designs [@forthmann2025; @goecke2024] and to rubric-coded responses to the PISA creative-thinking tasks [@myszkowski2025]. [\[FILL IN: verify pellegrino2025 (GRM retained), barbot2023 (model), forthmann2025 and goecke2024 (planned-missing designs) and myszkowski2025 (FI-17)\]]{.mark} We located no application to ratings of sport actions, apart from a Rasch analysis of a coach-completed questionnaire that rates players rather than actions [@shin2025]. Because the rating-scale and partial-credit models are constrained versions of the generalized partial credit model, the constraints become testable by model comparison instead of being imposed [@myszkowski2021]. Whether the flexibility of JRT is needed is therefore an empirical question.

## The present study

The present study analysed a large set of CAT-style creativity ratings of football actions given by 25 raters. Thousands of actions cannot each be rated by every rater, so the study used a pool-based sparse design, in which many raters each rate a subset of the actions and each action receives one to a few ratings [for planned-missing rating designs, see @primi2019; @forthmann2025; @goecke2024]. In such a design, the question of how many raters a panel needs becomes the question of how many ratings each action needs, and from which raters. The study was exploratory, and no confirmatory hypotheses were formulated. Three research questions were addressed.

- **RQ1 (number of ratings and reliability).** How reliable are the creativity scores obtained in this study, how does product-level reliability vary with the number of ratings an action received, and how many ratings per action are needed for reliable estimates in this rater pool, (a) as observed and (b) as simulated from the fitted model? How do these figures compare with a hypothetical full panel and with conventional agreement and consistency indices?
- **RQ2 (rater differences).** How do raters differ in severity, threshold location, scale use, discrimination and information, and how precisely are these differences estimated?
- **RQ3 (model constraints and consequences for scores).** (a) Are the Rasch-family constraints of a shared category structure and of equal discrimination tenable for these ratings? (b) How far do product scores and rankings depend on the scoring model, from the raw mean through the constrained models to the graded response model?

RQ1 addresses the first part of the question posed above, the number of ratings. RQ2 addresses the second part as far as these data allow: it asks how much the raters differ, and thus how much it matters which raters rate an action, not which raters should be chosen. RQ3 asks which model of the raters the answers require. Rater expertise and the design of the rating scale are not analysed.

The study makes four contributions. First, it compares four rater models on a nonverbal, time-pressured product class and tests whether rater-specific thresholds and rater-specific discrimination are needed. Second, it describes how far raw means and model-based scores order the actions differently when an action has one or two ratings, an indicative comparison that does not show which score is more accurate. Third, it describes reliability as a function of the number of ratings, observed and simulated, and reports the number of ratings at which simulated reliability reached .80 in this rater pool. Fourth, to our knowledge, it is the first study to adapt judge response theory to single actions in sport, which yields rater-adjusted scores with standard errors.

# Method

## Overview

This was a CAT-style rating study in which raters independently rated the creativity of football actions in a randomised order [@amabile1982; @hennessey2011]. [\[FILL IN: whether the raters were instructed to rate the actions relative to one another, as the CAT prescribes, or received no such instruction (FI-35)\]]{.mark} The ratings were collected as part of a larger project. [\[FILL IN: context and purpose of the larger project (FI-1)\]]{.mark} [\[FILL IN: ethics approval (committee, reference number) and informed-consent procedure (FI-1)\]]{.mark} The analyses were exploratory. [\[FILL IN: preregistration status (FI-15)\]]{.mark}

The procedure departed from the CAT in three respects. First, the raters were shown a definition of creativity, whereas the CAT gives raters no criteria [@hennessey2011]. Second, the design was sparse: each rater rated a subset of the actions, whereas in the CAT the raters usually rate all products. Third, whether the raters had the familiarity with the domain that the CAT requires was not established. The first two departures are described under Rating procedure and Rating design, and all three are taken up in the Limitations.

## Raters

The raters came from two pools. The first pool, raters R01–R19, consisted of Bachelor's and Master's students who rated as part of their thesis projects. [\[FILL IN: confirm; recruitment and number of raters at the start of the first pool (FI-1)\]]{.mark} The second pool comprised raters R23–R27 and R30. [\[FILL IN: background, recruitment and allocation of the second pool, raters R23–R27 and R30 (FI-31)\]]{.mark} [\[FILL IN: rater-pool description for both pools: football playing or coaching experience, any instruction or practice before rating, number of sessions per rater, demographics and compensation, or a statement that these were not recorded (FI-21)\]]{.mark} The final data comprised 25 raters, pseudonymised as R01–R19, R23–R27 and R30; the gaps in the numbering arise because five raters were excluded (see Data preparation and final data), and the numbers do not reflect the raters' workload. The raters gave between 47 and 1,174 ratings each (@tbl-design-summary).

## Products and stimulus material

Each rated product was a single football action; we use "product" for the analyses and "action" when referring to the football content. The actions came from matches of the men's and women's European Championships and World Cups, the Africa Cup of Nations and the Copa América. They were cut as short video clips and linked to event data [StatsBomb; @statsbomb2024]. [\[FILL IN: action-selection rule, clip length, video source and number of matches (FI-2)\]]{.mark} [\[FILL IN: check that statsbomb2024 is the intended reference for the event data (FI-17)\]]{.mark}

## Rating procedure

Ratings were collected with a browser-based, open-source rating app written in Streamlit (github.com/maxk92/streamlit-creativity-rating-app). Metadata and a pitch sketch identified each action, and the clip played in a loop. Three 7-point scales (creativity, technical correctness and aesthetic appeal) and an "action not recognised" option were shown with the clip. The order of the clips was randomised, familiarisation clips preceded the rating, the definition of creativity was available at any time during rating, and progress was saved per participant. [\[FILL IN: data-collection period as a sentence (FI-32)\]]{.mark} [\[FILL IN: session length and breaks, number of familiarisation clips, and the language version used by the raters; no timing statements for single raters (FI-34)\]]{.mark}

Before the familiarisation clips, the raters read a definition of creativity, in German or English, which follows the standard definition of creativity as originality and effectiveness [@stein1953; @runco2012]. In short, it describes a creative action in football as one that deviates from the norm, appears surprising and is potentially advantageous for one's own team, and it states that what matters is the intention or idea and the expected probability of success, not the actual outcome; the full text is given in the Supplementary Material (Definition of creativity shown to the raters). Showing a definition departs from the CAT rule that raters receive no criteria [@hennessey2011] and resembles the procedure of trained-rater studies in sport [@kempe2018; @memmert2010].

Creativity was rated on a unipolar 7-point scale with verbal labels at the endpoints only, 1 "not creative" and 7 "very creative". The rating-scale literature places the optimum at about seven categories [@preston2000; @lozano2008], and the scale was unipolar because creativity is an amount of a property, not a valence around a neutral point. [\[FILL IN: verify preston2000 and lozano2008 as sources for about seven categories (FI-17)\]]{.mark} Technical correctness and aesthetic appeal were rated on the same 7-point format so that construct validity can be examined later, as @amabile1982 recommends for a new domain; they are not analysed here. [\[FILL IN: verify the amabile1982 recommendation to rate further dimensions in a new domain (FI-17)\]]{.mark}

## Rating design

Actions were allocated to raters at random from the pool of actions. [\[FILL IN: the remaining details of the allocation: planned overlap between raters, any common or benchmark set, the allocation for the second rater pool, and how products came to have one, two or more ratings (FI-4)\]]{.mark} Not every rater rated every product, and most products received few ratings. The design was incomplete but connected: all raters and products formed a single connected component, so that all rater parameters and product scores lie on one scale [@eckes2015]. Marginal maximum likelihood estimation assumes that the missing ratings are ignorable given the design. Random allocation is in line with this assumption as far as it concerns which actions a rater rated; it does not by itself make the number of ratings a product received random. The distribution of the number of ratings per product is shown in @fig-design-ratings-per-product, the number of ratings per rater in @fig-overview-degree-distributions and the number of jointly rated products for each pair of raters in @fig-overview-rater-overlap, all in the supplement.

## Data preparation and final data

The raw export contained 11,323 rows. The 1,432 ratings marked "action not recognised" were removed; such ratings arise when video cutting, close-ups or other television artefacts leave the action not visible in the clip. [\[FILL IN: rate of "action not recognised" ratings by rater and, if available, by product (FI-22)\]]{.mark} One out-of-range value (0.0, given by R04) was removed. Twenty-six rater–product pairs had been entered more than once, one of them with conflicting values; the entry with the latest timestamp was kept, which removed 27 rows. This left 9,863 ratings by 30 raters.

Raters with fewer than 15 ratings were excluded because their up to seven rater-specific parameters cannot be estimated reliably: R20 (13 ratings), R21 (9), R22 (2), R28 (7) and R29 (1), together 32 ratings (@tbl-excluded-raters). [\[FILL IN: source or rationale for the exclusion criterion of 15 ratings (FI-23)\]]{.mark} One product rated only by these raters was dropped. The effect of the exclusion was examined by refitting the scoring model with the excluded raters; the result is reported under Model adequacy in the Results.

The final data are described in @tbl-design-summary: 9,831 ratings of 3,841 products by 25 raters, given on the scale 1–7 and coded 0–6 internally. Products received a mean of 2.559 ratings (median 2, range 1–14, harmonic mean 1.819), and 857 products received a single rating. The product-by-rater matrix had a fill of .102 and formed one connected component; 23 of the 300 rater pairs had no product in common, and the median overlap of rater pairs was 22.5 products. Eight raters left at least one category unused (@tbl-category-usage in the supplement): category 7 was never used by R01, R03, R06, R18, R25 and R26, categories 6 and 7 were never used by R17, and categories 5 and 7 were never used by R27, so that R27 has an unused category inside the observed range (an internal gap). Because thresholds are estimated only between categories a rater used, R17 and R27 have four thresholds, R01, R03, R06, R18, R25 and R26 five, and all other raters six. The thresholds of R27 separate other category boundaries than those of the other raters and are not directly comparable with them.

## Measurement models

Item response theory models the probability of each response as a function of a latent attribute and of item parameters [@lord1980; @embretson2013; @ayala2022]. Among its polytomous models, the rating scale model [RSM; @andrich1978] and the partial credit model [PCM; @masters1982] belong to the Rasch family, which constrains all items to discriminate equally [@rasch1960; @bond2020], and differ in whether all items share one category structure, whereas the generalized partial credit model [@muraki1992] and the graded response model [@samejima1969] add item-specific discrimination; the first three model the odds of adjacent categories, and the graded response model models the cumulative probability of a response above each category.

All models here share the JRT frame [@myszkowski2019; @myszkowski2021]: raters take the role of items, products the role of persons, and product creativity is a single latent dimension $\theta$ with a normal distribution and a mean of 0. Its variance was fixed at 1 in the two models with rater-specific discriminations and estimated in the two Rasch-family models, whose discriminations are fixed. The discrimination $a$ expresses how sharply a rater's ratings separate products of different creativity. In the graded response model, a rater's threshold $b_k$ is the $\theta$ at which a rating above category $k$ becomes more likely than a rating of $k$ or below; the adjacent-category models have step parameters instead, each the $\theta$ at which two adjacent categories are equally likely. Because the cumulative probabilities of the graded response model depend on $a(\theta - b_k)$, the same differences in category use correspond to more widely spaced thresholds when the discrimination is low; threshold spacing and discrimination are therefore not separate facts about a rater.

Four models were fitted, each with raters as items: M1, the rating-scale many-facet Rasch model; M2, the partial-credit MFRM; M3, the generalized partial credit model; GRM, the graded response model. M1, M2 and M3 form a ladder of nested adjacent-category models. M1 was the rating scale model with a rater severity parameter, which corresponds to a two-facet many-facet Rasch model with a shared rating scale when products and raters are the facets [@linacre1989; @eckes2015; @primi2019]; it was estimated by marginal maximum likelihood with a normal product distribution in `sirt::rm.facets` [@robitzsch2025]. M1 is the only model in the ladder in which all raters share one category structure. M2 was the partial credit model with rater-specific thresholds, which corresponds to a many-facet Rasch model with a rater-specific category structure [@eckes2015]; like every Rasch model, it assumes equal discrimination. M3 additionally gives each rater their own discrimination. M2 and M3 were estimated with the R package mirt [@chalmers2012].

The product scores of all analyses come from the GRM, with rater-specific discriminations and thresholds, estimated in mirt. Its thresholds are ordered by construction, and a cumulative link is plausible for a unipolar scale. It also had the lowest Akaike information criterion (AIC) and sample-size adjusted Bayesian information criterion (SABIC) of the four models and a Bayesian information criterion (BIC) within 0.416 of the lowest (see the model comparison under RQ3 in the Results). The GRM was estimated by marginal maximum likelihood with the expectation–maximisation (EM) algorithm (61 quadrature points, tolerance 0.0001), with standard errors from Oakes' identity [@chalmers2018]; the settings are listed in @tbl-grm-convergence in the supplement.

## Model comparison

Two likelihood-ratio (LR) tests were computed within the ladder: M1 against M2 for a shared against a rater-specific category structure, and M2 against M3 for equal against rater-specific discriminations. For all four models, the log-likelihood, AIC, BIC and SABIC were computed, with the difference to the best model on each criterion. BIC penalises each parameter by the logarithm of the sample size and thus, at this sample size, more heavily than AIC. [\[FILL IN: which sample size enters the BIC and SABIC penalties in mirt and in sirt, the number of products or the number of ratings (FI-36)\]]{.mark} The GRM, which is not nested in the ladder, was compared by information criteria only. Three caveats apply. The M1–M2 test compares models estimated in different software (sirt and mirt), so it is approximate. Its degrees of freedom (110) lie below the formula value $(J-1)(K-2) = 120$ for $J$ raters and $K$ categories, because the observed degrees of freedom are smaller by the number of categories raters never used, that is, unused end categories and any internal gap (@tbl-category-usage); the internal gap of R27 also makes the nesting of M1 in M2 approximate. Finally, no model without rater effects was fitted, so severity differences were not tested on their own.

## Model adequacy

Infit and outfit mean squares [@wright1982] were computed for each rater under M1 and the GRM. Their expected value is 1. For the GRM, values outside 0.7–1.3 are flagged in the rater overview (@tbl-rater-overview in the supplement); with about two ratings per product, values below 1 are expected, because each product's score is estimated from the very ratings being checked, so flags below 0.7 are read as a property of the design rather than as misfit, and no further cut-offs were applied. The M1 values are reported without flags. The S-X² statistic [@orlando2000; @kang2008] requires complete data, so the missing ratings were imputed 20 times from the fitted model and the statistic was averaged. About 90% of the cells were imputed, so the test is conservative. Local dependence was examined with Yen's Q3 [@yen1984], the correlation of two raters' residuals over the products both rated. Q3 was computed for rater pairs with at least three jointly rated products (256 of the 300 pairs were computable). Because Q3 is negatively biased when few raters rate each product [@christensen2017], pairs were compared by their deviation from the mean Q3 over all computable pairs. A pair was flagged when it had at least 30 jointly rated products and deviated from this mean by more than 0.2. This criterion has no reference distribution. The global statistic C2 [@cai2014] could not be computed, because it needs the joint distribution of every rater pair and 23 of the 300 pairs share no products.

## Scores, reliability and the two simulations

Product scores were expected a posteriori (EAP) estimates $\hat\theta$ with the posterior standard deviation (PSD) as their standard error. The primary index was the empirical reliability of the obtained scores, $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta) / [\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta) + \overline{\mathrm{PSD}^2}]$, which the tables call empirical marginal reliability. For comparison, the model-based full-panel reliability [@green1984], which refers to a hypothetical product rated by all raters and which the tables call model-based marginal reliability, was computed with mirt and checked on a $\theta$ grid. Ninety-five percent intervals for both came from 200 accepted draws of the parameters from their asymptotic normal distribution (estimates and Oakes covariance matrix); for the empirical reliability, products were also resampled. A draw that did not define a valid GRM (some $a \leq 0$ or thresholds out of order) was rejected and replaced; 53 draws were rejected. The intervals are therefore conditional on valid parameter sets and approximate, especially for raters with few ratings.

At the product level, the product-level reliability rel~post~ $= 1 - \mathrm{PSD}^2$ was computed. Because it is defined relative to the unit prior variance of $\theta$, it partly reflects the prior when a product has one or two ratings. As a check, rel~info~ $= I/(I+1)$ was computed from the information $I$ of the product's own raters at $\hat\theta$. Both were summarised by the number of ratings each product received.

Conventional reliability indices assume a complete design or must be adapted to an incomplete one [@hove2024], so we report them only as reference values for common practice. Cronbach's alpha [@cronbach1951] was computed from pairwise covariances over all usable raters and on the largest fully crossed block of raters and products [\[FILL IN: why seven raters (R26, R12, R19, R14, R02, R27, R17) were not usable for the pairwise alpha; which three raters form the crossed block (FI-9)\]]{.mark}, and Krippendorff's ordinal alpha [@hayes2007] measured the agreement of single ratings. The number of jointly rated products of each rater pair, on which the pairwise covariances rest, is shown in @fig-overview-rater-overlap. Ninety-five percent confidence intervals came from bootstrapping products (1,000 replications). For the pairwise alpha, 513 of the 1,000 replications could be computed; in the other 487, some rater pair lost all shared products. The interval rests on the computable replications and is approximate and possibly biased.

Two simulations from the fitted GRM addressed the number of ratings needed (RQ1b). The criterion was a reliability of .80, the value used as the target in the generalizability studies cited above [@silvia2008; @kaufman2007; @hass2018], where it is a person-level generalizability or phi target; here it is applied to the reliability of product scores.

In the projection, products with $\theta \sim N(0, 1)$ were simulated; each received $k$ ratings ($k$ = 1 to 10) from $k$ distinct raters of the panel drawn at random, each rater being equally likely to be drawn, so that the draws do not reproduce the raters' actual workloads in the study. Ratings were generated from the fitted GRM and scored with its parameters, which were treated as known. The projection used 50 replications of 2,000 simulated products per $k$ (seed 20260713) and gave, for each $k$, the mean and the 95% range over replications of the empirical reliability of the simulated scores, which we call simulated reliability from here on, and the mean rel~post~; the smallest $k$ at which the simulated reliability reached .80 is reported.

The top-up simulation was built on the actual design: it kept the actual assignment of raters to products, that is, which raters had rated which product, but not the ratings themselves. It was run for the actual design, in which each product kept its raters, and for a design with at least four ratings per product, in which every product with fewer than four ratings was in addition assigned raters drawn at random with equal probability and without replacement from the panel raters who had not rated it, until it had four; products with four or more ratings were unchanged. In each of 50 replications, every real product received a creativity value $\theta$ drawn from $N(0, 1)$, all ratings in the design, for the kept and the added rater–product pairs alike, were generated from the fitted GRM, and the products were scored by EAP with the parameters treated as known. The real ratings were not reused; the actual-design row is a validation of the simulation, which should reproduce the empirical reliability of the obtained scores. In both simulations the ranges reflect simulation variability only, not parameter uncertainty, and the observed data remain primary. Observed and simulated values are shown side by side in @fig-grm-reliability-observed-vs-simulated and in @tbl-grm-reliability-observed-vs-simulated in the supplement; they are different quantities, the observed mean rel~post~ of the actual products and the simulated reliability.

## Rater parameters, severity, information and response styles

Rater severity under M1 was reported with its standard error (0 = average rater, higher = stricter), and the GRM discrimination $a$ and thresholds $b_k$ of each rater with their standard errors; intervals for $a$ are ±1.96 *SE*. Rater information integrated over the standard normal distribution of $\theta$ is called the rater's average information; each rater's share of the full-panel information was computed overall and at selected values of $\theta$, with 95% intervals from the same parameter draws as above (@tbl-grm-rater-information-ci and @tbl-grm-information-summary in the supplement). Descriptive response styles were computed on the raw 1–7 scale (@tbl-overview-rater-response-styles in the supplement); they are not adjusted for which products each rater saw and carry no per-rater uncertainty. @tbl-rater-overview in the supplement collects the main quantities per rater.

## Score agreement and sensitivity

Each product's raw mean rating, the common-practice score that treats raters as interchangeable, was compared with its GRM score separately for products with one, two, and three or more ratings. Because the raw mean takes few distinct values (with one rating, only seven), agreement was described by Kendall's $\tau_b$, by the share of product pairs with different raw means that the GRM score orders the other way round (pairs in reversed order), and by the mean and maximum range of GRM scores among products with the same raw mean. To describe the dependence on the choice among the four models, the EAP scores of all models were correlated (Pearson and Spearman); relative to the GRM, the absolute shift in percentile rank (0–1 scale) and the share of products changing quintile were computed. M1 was also re-estimated with the default integration grid of sirt as a check. The empirical reliability of the scores was computed for each of the four models (@tbl-marginal-reliability-models in the supplement). Finally, as a check on the rater exclusion, the GRM was refitted with all raters who could be estimated (29 raters; R29, who gave one rating, could not be estimated).

## Software and availability

All models were estimated in R with mirt [@chalmers2012] and sirt [@robitzsch2025]; psych and an R package for Krippendorff's alpha were used for the conventional indices, and Python for display. [\[FILL IN: versions of R, mirt, sirt and psych, and the name and version of the package used for Krippendorff's alpha (FI-6)\]]{.mark} The rating app is available from the repository named under Rating procedure. [\[FILL IN: data and code availability statement; only pseudonymised rater IDs are shared (FI-15)\]]{.mark}

# Results

The results follow the three research questions: the reliability of the scores and the number of ratings (RQ1), the differences between raters (RQ2), and the tenability of the model constraints and their consequences for the scores (RQ3). All analyses used the final data in @tbl-design-summary. We first report the adequacy of the GRM.

## Model adequacy

The GRM converged after 550 EM iterations with a positive definite information matrix (@tbl-grm-convergence). No rater's S-X² was significant (*p* from .362 to .601; @tbl-grm-rater-fit). Infit ranged from 0.315 (R26) to 0.983 (R18) and outfit from 0.303 (R26) to 0.973 (R18), all below 1; 14 raters were flagged in @tbl-rater-overview, all for values below 0.7 (for R15 and R01, whose outfit appears as 0.70 there, @tbl-grm-rater-fit gives 0.697 and 0.698). The mean Q3 over the 256 computable pairs was −.188, and 36 pairs were flagged; of the 10 shown in @tbl-grm-q3-flagged, eight deviated negatively and two (R09–R23 and R17–R24) positively, and R02 was part of five. C2 could not be computed (see Model adequacy in the Method). Refitting the GRM with 29 raters (9,862 ratings, 3,842 products) gave scores that correlated at *r* = .99997 with those of the final fit over the 3,841 common products, with a maximum absolute difference of 0.16518; the reliabilities and the discriminations of the two fits are compared in @tbl-sensitivity-rater-exclusion.

## Reliability of the scores and number of ratings (RQ1)

@tbl-reliability-overview sets the reliability of the obtained scores against the other indices and states what each refers to. The empirical reliability of the obtained scores was .695 \[.673, .711\]. The model-based full-panel reliability, which refers to a hypothetical product rated by all raters, was .970 \[.966, .973\], with a grid check of .970 (@tbl-grm-reliability-ci; @fig-grm-panel-information); both intervals are conditional on valid parameter draws (see Scores, reliability and the two simulations). Cronbach's alpha from pairwise covariances, which refers to the consistency of the unweighted rater mean, was .959 \[.931, .970\] (18 raters, 1,948 products); its interval is approximate, because it rests on the 513 of 1,000 bootstrap replications that could be computed (@tbl-naive-indices). On the fully crossed block, Cronbach's alpha was .785 \[.736, .823\] (3 raters, 270 products). Krippendorff's ordinal alpha, which refers to the agreement of single ratings, was .402 \[.375, .427\] (25 raters, 2,984 products).

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/03_jrt_supplement.ipynb#tbl-reliability-overview >}}

@tbl-grm-reliability-by-n summarises the observed product-level reliability by the number of ratings each product received. Mean rel~post~ was .526 for the 857 products with one rating, .703 for the 2,227 with two, .770 for the 73 with three and .815 for the 93 with four, the first row at or above .80. It rose further to .955 at 14 ratings, with one exception: .915 at 10 ratings after .917 at nine. No mean reached the model-based full-panel reliability of .970. Products with the same number of ratings differed in rel~post~ (@fig-grm-rel-post-by-n). These values are observed: although actions were allocated to raters at random, the number of ratings a product received was not manipulated (see Rating design). [\[FILL IN: how products came to have their number of ratings (FI-4)\]]{.mark}

@fig-grm-reliability-observed-vs-simulated places the observed means next to the simulated reliability of the projection; the values are given in @tbl-grm-reliability-projection and @tbl-grm-reliability-observed-vs-simulated in the supplement (see also @fig-grm-reliability-projection). The simulated reliability rose at every step, from .526 \[.511, .538\] at one rating to .702 \[.691, .712\] at two, .785 \[.776, .793\] at three, .832 \[.825, .838\] at four and .928 \[.925, .932\] at 10; the smallest number of ratings at which simulated reliability reached .80 was four. The observed means lay inside the simulated 95% range at one, two and nine ratings, below it at three, four, five, seven, eight and 10 ratings, and at its lower bound at six (.879).

The top-up simulation is reported in @tbl-grm-reliability-min-ratings in the supplement; its second design also appears as a row of @tbl-reliability-overview. For the actual design, the simulated reliability was .691 \[.684, .699\] (mean rel~post~ .693), next to the observed .695 of the obtained scores. For the design with at least four ratings per product, with 7,098 rater–product pairs added in 3,157 products (16,929 simulated ratings in total), it was .837 \[.832, .842\].

Across all products, rel~post~ had a median of .706 and an interquartile range of .195 (first and third quartiles .601 and .796), with values from .071 to .955 (@tbl-grm-reliability-summary; @fig-grm-rel-post-histogram); its relation to $\hat\theta$ is shown in @fig-grm-rel-post-by-theta. rel~post~ and rel~info~ correlated at *r* = .947, and 274 products differed by more than .1 (@fig-grm-rel-consistency).

## Rater differences (RQ2)

@fig-category-usage-shares shows how each rater used the seven categories; the response-style values are given in @tbl-overview-rater-response-styles and @fig-overview-rater-response-styles in the supplement. Rater means ranged from 1.760 (R06) to 4.012 (R19) and standard deviations from 1.022 (R01) to 1.841 (R02). The share of ratings in the lowest category (1) ranged from .579 (R06) to .016 (R13), and the share in the highest category (7) was highest for R19 (.064). The share in the middle categories (3–5) was highest for R13 (.799), followed by R18 (.764) and R12 (.735), and lowest for R06 (.192). Entropy ranged from 1.191 (R06) to 1.903 (R09; mean rating 3.643). Across all ratings, category 1 received 2,278 ratings and category 2 received 2,501; frequencies fell from category 2 to category 7, which received 149 (@fig-overview-rating-distribution). These response-style values are descriptive and have no per-rater uncertainty.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#fig-category-usage-shares >}}

@fig-m1-rater-severity shows the severity of each rater under M1 with its 95% interval next to the rater's raw mean; the values are given in @tbl-rater-overview in the supplement. Severity ranged from −1.005 (*SE* 0.059, R19) to 1.383 (*SE* 0.058, R06), a span of 2.388 logits; R19 also had the highest and R06 the lowest raw mean. The order of the severities did not follow the order of the raw means exactly: R14 had a higher raw mean (2.22) than R01 (2.16), R17 (2.08) and R27 (2.06) but also a higher severity (0.84 against 0.76, 0.68 and 0.80), the second-highest after R06.

@tbl-grm-rater-parameters gives the GRM parameters with their standard errors; the category response functions are shown in @fig-grm-category-response-functions in the supplement. Over all 25 raters, the first threshold $b_1$ ranged from −6.39 (R18, 55 ratings, *SE* 2.92) to 0.24 (R06, *SE* 0.05); the next lowest was −3.43 (R13, *SE* 0.49), and R06 was the only rater with a positive $b_1$. Threshold spacing also differed, for example from −0.68 ($b_1$) to 2.02 ($b_6$) for R02 and from −3.43 to 4.39 for R13; spacing depends on discrimination (see Measurement models). The number of thresholds per rater follows from the categories the rater used (see Data preparation and final data), and the thresholds of R27 are not compared with those of the other raters.

The next highest values came from raters with many ratings as well as few: R06 3.15 (520 ratings, *SE* 0.45), R25 3.03 (138, *SE* 0.45), R12 2.91 (264, *SE* 0.50) and R27 2.85 (47, *SE* 0.82); the next lowest was R09 at 0.95 (400 ratings, *SE* 0.15). The largest standard errors of $a$ belonged to R26 (1.49), R27 (0.82) and R30 (0.69, 47 ratings).

Average information is shown with 95% intervals, based on the same 200 accepted parameter draws, in @fig-grm-rater-information-ci; the values and the information shares are given in @tbl-grm-rater-information-ci in the supplement. Average information ranged from 0.13 \[0.00, 0.37\] (R18) to 3.96 \[0.66, 8.40\] (R26), and shares from .004 \[.000, .011\] (R18) to .112 \[.021, .205\] (R26). The widest intervals belonged to R26, R27 and R30. Raters provided information in different regions of the latent scale (@fig-grm-rater-information; @tbl-grm-information-summary). The location of maximum information was highest for R01 (2.850), R16 (2.550) and R06 (2.300) and lowest for R13 (−0.600). Shares varied with $\theta$ (@fig-grm-information-shares): R06 contributed .001 of the panel information at $\theta = -2$ and .078 at $\theta = 2$, whereas the largest shares at $\theta = -2$ came from R12 (.151), R24 (.107) and R15 (.105). All intervals in this section are conditional on valid parameter draws.

## Model constraints and consequences for the scores (RQ3)

The LR test of M1 against M2, which concerns the shared category structure of M1, gave $\chi^2(110) = 878.581$, *p* \< .001 (@tbl-lr-tests in the supplement; @tbl-model-fit); AIC was lower for M2 (29,764.582 vs. 30,423.163), whereas BIC was lower for M1 (30,617.021 vs. 30,646.324, a difference of 29.303). The test of M2 against M3, which concerns equal discrimination, gave $\chi^2(24) = 177.440$, *p* \< .001; AIC was lower for M3 (29,635.141 vs. 29,764.582), whereas BIC was lower for M2 (30,646.324 vs. 30,666.967). Both constraints were thus rejected by the LR test and AIC but not by BIC. The GRM had the lowest AIC (29,585.612) and SABIC (30,093.144) of the four models. It has the same number of parameters as M3 (165), with a log-likelihood of −14,627.806 against −14,652.571, and was lower than M3 by 49.530 on AIC and on SABIC. On BIC, M1 (30,617.021) and the GRM (30,617.437) differed by 0.416. The four models had 31 (M1), 141 (M2), 165 (M3) and 165 (GRM) parameters.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-model-fit >}}

Within the ladder, the M3 discriminations ranged from 0.298 (R18, *SE* 0.138) to 3.056 (R26, *SE* 1.372), with a median of 1.213, a ratio of the largest to the smallest of 10.254 and a standard deviation of 0.634 (@tbl-discrimination-m3; @tbl-discrimination-summary). Nine raters had unordered step parameters under M2 and eight under M3 (@tbl-threshold-order). Under M1, infit and outfit were above 1 for R09 (infit 1.147, outfit 1.123), R17 (1.371, 1.182), R18 (1.233, 1.307) and R30 (1.136, 1.051); for R11, only the infit was above 1 (infit 1.011, outfit 0.954). Of these values, only the infit of R17 and the outfit of R18 lay above 1.3. R12 had the lowest values (0.259, 0.276; @tbl-rater-fit-m1).

@tbl-raw-mean-vs-grm and @fig-raw-mean-vs-theta compare each product's raw mean rating with its GRM score within groups of products with the same number of ratings. For the 857 products with one rating, Kendall's $\tau_b$ was .773, and .076 of the pairs with different raw means were in reversed order. Products with the same single rating received GRM scores that spanned on average 1.240 and at most 1.420 on the GRM score scale; in the one-rating panel of @fig-raw-mean-vs-theta, this appears as vertical spread at each rating (points are jittered horizontally). For the 2,227 products with two ratings, $\tau_b$ was .818, .066 of the pairs were in reversed order, and the range of GRM scores at equal raw mean was 1.558 on average and 2.129 at most. For the 757 products with three or more ratings, the values were .861, .065, 0.507 and 1.306. Kendall's $\tau_b$ thus rose and the share of pairs in reversed order fell from one rating to two and to three or more, and the largest range at equal raw mean occurred with two ratings.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#fig-raw-mean-vs-theta >}}

@tbl-score-agreement compares the scores of the constrained models with the GRM scores. Relative to the GRM, M1 scores correlated at .978 (Pearson) and .980 (Spearman), and .188 of products changed quintile, with a mean percentile shift of .040. For M2, the correlations were .986 and .984, and .155 of products changed quintile, with a mean percentile shift of .032; for M3, they were .996 and .997, and .073 changed quintile, with a mean percentile shift of .016. Among the ladder models, Pearson correlations ranged from .982 to .993 and Spearman correlations from .985 to .996 (@tbl-theta-correlations); M1 re-estimated with the default integration grid correlated at 1.000 with M1. The empirical reliability of the scores was .663 for M1, .669 for M2, .682 for M3 and .695 for the GRM (@tbl-marginal-reliability-models); these differences were not tested.

# Discussion

## RQ1: Reliability and the number of ratings per action

The obtained scores were far less reliable than the panel as a whole (.695 against a model-based full-panel reliability of .970), and four ratings per action were needed for a simulated reliability of .80. We read this gap as a property of the design, not of the raters. With the same raters and the same fitted parameters, and under the assumptions stated in the Method, simulated reliability was .691 for the actual assignment of raters to actions and .837 once every action had at least four ratings (top-up simulation), and it reached .928 with 10 ratings per action (projection). These values are implied by the fitted model, in which reliability rises with the number of ratings by construction; they describe the size of the design effect under the model and are not independent evidence for it. The full-panel figure describes a product that every rater rated, which no product in these data was. This is the Spearman–Brown logic described by @amabile1982: the model-based full-panel reliability and Cronbach's alpha refer to more ratings per product than the products received. What the raters contribute is the level of reliability at a given number of ratings. Single ratings agreed at a Krippendorff's alpha of .402, while the pairwise Cronbach's alpha, an approximate value that rests on 18 of the 25 raters, was .959. By the same logic alpha rises with the number of raters, and consistency is not absolute agreement, a distinction that is seldom drawn in creativity research [@stefanic2015; @cseh2019]. The empirical reliability of the obtained scores is therefore the figure that matters when the scores are used. [\[FILL IN: verify the stefanic2015 and cseh2019 attributions (FI-17)\]]{.mark}

Where individual action scores are used, for example to select creative actions, one or two ratings per action gave limited precision in these data (mean rel~post~ .526 and .703). The observed means reached .80 at four ratings (.815, 93 products), the same number as in the simulation; from three ratings on, the observed means lay at or below the simulated range, except at nine ratings. Several readings of this difference are possible: the observed mean rel~post~ and the simulated reliability are defined differently (see Scores, reliability and the two simulations), the products with several ratings were rated by particular raters rather than by random draws from the panel, and some of the rows rest on few products. [\[FILL IN: whether products with different numbers of ratings were rated by different raters (FI-4)\]]{.mark} The data do not decide between these readings. The values by number of ratings are observational: actions were allocated to raters at random, but how an action came to have its number of ratings was not manipulated. Precision also differed among products with the same number of ratings and with their location on $\theta$ (@fig-grm-rel-post-by-n; @fig-grm-rel-post-by-theta), and for one or two ratings, rel~post~ partly reflects the prior.

Read against the cross-domain evidence, with the reliability target and the object of measurement stated, four ratings for .80 in these product-level scores from this rater pool can be set beside the two or three trained raters projected for short divergent-thinking responses, measured at the person level against a relative generalizability coefficient of .80 [@silvia2008], the finding that 10 novices did not reach an adequate Cronbach's alpha for expert-domain products, where panels of 10 expert writers and 15 professional engineers did [@kaufman2008a; @kaufman2013], and the 7 to 15 non-experts needed for fashion and design products against intraclass correlations of .70 [@barth2021; @terai2026]. The sport studies cited in the Introduction used panels of three or four expert raters and reported the agreement of the panel [@kempe2018; @joode2023; @memmert2010; @roca2018]. Their figures are thus panel figures, not figures for the number of ratings needed for a target reliability; whether coaches need fewer ratings than this rater pool is untested here, because rater expertise was not analysed.

## RQ2: Raters differ

Raters differed in severity, scale use, discrimination and information, and some of these differences were imprecisely estimated, for raters with about 50 ratings and for R26, who had 136. Severity under M1 spanned 2.388 logits, from R19 to R06. This span is larger than the ranges @primi2019 report for metaphor and divergent-thinking ratings (−1.18 to .64 logits in their first study and about 0.9 in their second), although their ratings used other scales, rating formats and raters, so that logit spans are only indicatively comparable; severity differences of this size confound raw means whenever different raters rate different actions [@primi2019; @hass2018]. [\[FILL IN: verify the primi2019 severity ranges (FI-17)\]]{.mark} For raters with many ratings, the differences in discrimination clearly exceeded the standard errors, for example between R09 ($a$ = 0.95, *SE* 0.15) and R06 (3.15, *SE* 0.45). High discrimination was not confined to imprecisely estimated raters (R06, R25 and R12 had 520, 138 and 264 ratings), so the spread in discrimination is not mainly estimation noise. The largest standard errors belonged to R18 for its thresholds and to R26, R27 and R30 for their discriminations. R27 and R30 had 47 ratings, but R26 had 136, so a larger number of ratings did not by itself give a precise discrimination estimate here. The information shares are not a ranking of rater quality: they depend on the parameters as estimated, and for some raters these are poorly determined. Read literally, one rating by the most informative rater (3.96) carries as much information as many ratings by the least informative (0.13), but the interval of the former runs from 0.66 to 8.40.

Because threshold spacing in the GRM depends on discrimination (see Measurement models), the raw response styles (@tbl-overview-rater-response-styles) carry the model-independent evidence on scale use, although they are not adjusted for which products each rater saw. Eight raters never used the top category, and R27 left a category inside the observed range unused. These differences are in line with reports of differing scale use and beliefs among CAT raters [@long2015] and with the rater effects described in rater-mediated assessment [@engelhard1994; @myford2003; @myford2004]. The contrast between raters who concentrated their ratings in the middle categories (e.g., R13) and raters who used the lowest category heavily (e.g., R06) corresponds to the central versus extreme responding discussed by @myszkowski2021; @primi2019 left such rater-by-scale interactions to future research. [\[FILL IN: verify the attributions to myszkowski2021 and primi2019 (FI-17)\]]{.mark} That the estimates of some raters are imprecise agrees with work showing that rater estimates in incomplete rating networks depend on the linking set [@wind2018; @wind2019] and that parameter recovery in the graded response model requires adequate numbers of responses [@reise1990]. [\[FILL IN: verify the attributions to wind2018, wind2019 and reise1990 (FI-17)\]]{.mark}

These results answer the second half of the question, from whom the ratings should come, only in part. The raters were not interchangeable: with a severity span of 2.388 logits and one or two ratings per action, which raters rated an action shifted its raw mean. The data do not, however, support selecting raters: the information shares are not a ranking of rater quality, the parameters of the most extreme raters were imprecise, no selected rater sets were simulated, and rater expertise was not analysed. In these data, "from whom" is therefore a matter of linking the raters and adjusting for their differences, not of choosing among them.

## RQ3: Constraints and consequences for scoring

The Rasch-family constraints were rejected by the LR tests and AIC but not by BIC, and, in an indicative comparison, the choice among the four models changed the ordering of actions less than the choice between the GRM and the raw mean. The scores of M1, M2 and M3 correlated with the GRM scores at Spearman's $\rho$ = .980 to .997, and the empirical reliability of the scores was similar across the four models (.663 to .695). Raw means and GRM scores, by contrast, agreed at $\tau_b$ = .773 to .861 within groups of products with equal numbers of ratings, with .065 to .076 of pairs in reversed order, and products with the same raw mean lay up to 2.129 apart on the GRM score scale. This range reflects differences in both the threshold location and the discrimination of the raters who gave the ratings and, with two or more ratings, the combinations of ratings behind the same mean. Two caveats apply. First, the raw mean was compared with the GRM scores only, and $\tau_b$ on a heavily tied score is not the same statistic as Spearman's $\rho$ over all products, so the contrast is indicative. Second, none of these comparisons shows that model-based scores are more accurate than raw means or than the constrained models: the GRM adjusts for the modelled rater differences under its assumptions, but whether it predicts unseen ratings better was not examined, and it is not a validated criterion. Unweighted means treat raters as interchangeable, and when different raters rate different actions, the means are confounded with rater severity [@primi2019; @myszkowski2019]. With one rating, a product's GRM score depends only on that rating and on the parameters of the rater who gave it, and this is where agreement with the raw mean was lowest ($\tau_b$ = .773; .076 of pairs in reversed order). Wherever actions are selected or ranked, for example to compile the most creative actions for training material, such reversals matter.

The shared category structure concerns M1 only; M2 already allows each rater their own category structure [@eckes2015]. Equal discrimination is the constraint shared by the whole Rasch family. On both constraints the criteria disagreed: the LR tests and AIC rejected them, whereas BIC was lowest for M1, and the GRM, with 165 parameters against 31, lay 0.416 above it, which we read as a practical tie. The disagreement follows from the criteria themselves: BIC penalises each additional parameter more heavily than AIC (see Model comparison), which weighs against the rater-specific parameters of M2 and M3 (141 and 165 parameters against 31). The M3 discriminations spanned 0.298 to 3.056, a ratio of 10.254. The M1 fit values are largely consistent with the account that, in Rasch-family models, differences in discrimination surface only as misfit [@myford2004; @myszkowski2021]: the three raters with the lowest M3 discriminations (R18, R09 and R17) had M1 infit and outfit above 1, and the two raters with the highest M3 discriminations (R26 and R12) had the two lowest M1 infit values (@tbl-discrimination-m3; @tbl-rater-fit-m1). Two raters do not fit the account: R30, whose M3 discrimination lay above the median, also had M1 infit and outfit above 1, and R11 had an M1 infit just above 1 with an outfit below it. The account is therefore illustrative. Neither the unordered steps in M2 and M3 nor the ordered GRM thresholds count as evidence for either model family, because unordered steps indicate only that some category is never the most likely response [@andrich1978; @bond2020]. [\[FILL IN: verify that andrich1978 and bond2020 carry this reading of unordered steps; Andrich is usually cited for the position that disordered thresholds signal a problem with the categories (FI-17)\]]{.mark}

The choice among the models still shifted some rankings: although all correlations with the GRM were .978 or higher, .188 of products changed quintile under M1, with a mean percentile shift of .040, and .073 under M3, with a mean percentile shift of .016. A quintile change can also be a small move across a quintile boundary, so the two measures are best read together. Because the M1–GRM contrast combines the rater constraints with a change of link function, the two sources cannot be separated here.

## Designing creativity-rating studies for nonverbal, time-pressured products

The implications are drawn from one rater pool, one 7-point scale and one product class. [\[FILL IN: rater-pool description to qualify this scope (FI-21)\]]{.mark} Two points go beyond the single results. First, the number of ratings needed could not have been read off the existing evidence: the published figures come from other material, targets and objects, and the figure found here, four ratings for .80 in this rater pool, differs from them for reasons that these data cannot separate (domain, rater pool, scale, target and object). To our knowledge, this study supplies the first rating-design figures for football actions; rating-design evidence for nonverbal, time-pressured products therefore has to be collected, not assumed, all the more because the number of raters needed is still among the open questions of the CAT [@cseh2019]. Second, in a pool-based sparse design the design decision is the number of ratings per action and the linking of the raters, not the size of a panel. In these ratings of actions observed in competition, single ratings agreed weakly (Krippendorff's alpha .402) while raters differed strongly in severity, scale use and discrimination, so in such a pool, panels of three or four raters without a rater model would carry unquantified rater effects. For a study of this size the consequence is considerable: bringing every action to at least four ratings would have taken 7,098 further ratings in 3,157 of the 3,841 actions, that is, 16,929 ratings instead of 9,831. Who should give these ratings cannot be said from these data, because coaches or other football experts were not compared with this rater pool. The recommendations that follow from these points are summarised in the box.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Design recommendations for creativity ratings of actions in sport"}
1.  Report the reliability of the scores actually used and the agreement of single ratings, not only alpha or full-panel values (see @tbl-reliability-overview: .695 against a pairwise Cronbach's alpha of .959, which rests on 18 raters, and a model-based full-panel reliability of .970; Krippendorff's alpha .402).
2.  Plan the number of ratings per action with the precision of single scores in mind: one or two ratings gave .526 and .703 here, and in this rater pool the smallest number of ratings at which simulated reliability reached .80 was four (see @tbl-grm-reliability-by-n and @fig-grm-reliability-observed-vs-simulated).
3.  Let all raters rate a sufficiently large common calibration set of actions, so that raters are linked and the parameters of raters with few ratings are estimated more precisely (the present design was connected; [\[FILL IN: confirm that no set of actions was rated by all raters; the largest fully crossed block comprised three raters and 270 actions (FI-4)\]]{.mark}).
4.  Report the standard errors of the rater parameters and do not rely on the number of ratings per rater alone: that number did not by itself determine precision here, where some parameters of raters with about 50 ratings were very imprecise, yet the least precise discrimination belonged to a rater with 136 ratings (see @tbl-grm-rater-parameters). These data give no minimum number of ratings per rater.
5.  Consider scoring actions with a model that adjusts for rater differences, under that model's assumptions, and report how far its ordering departs from the raw mean (see @fig-m1-rater-severity and @tbl-raw-mean-vs-grm). In an indicative comparison, the choice among such models changed the ordering less here than the choice between the GRM and the raw mean. This study does not show that model-based scores are more accurate.
6.  Treat these figures as specific to this product class, rater pool and scale; rating-design figures from this or other material cannot be assumed to hold for other nonverbal, time-pressured products, rater pools or scales.
:::

Two of the recommendations need a comment. A common calibration set of actions rated by all raters (recommendation 3) is distinct from rater training. Training imposes criteria on the raters, which the CAT avoids [@hennessey2011; @dollinger2005; @storme2014], and the definition shown in this study already departs from that rule (see Overview in the Method); a calibration set adds no criteria, and it stabilises the parameters of raters with few ratings only if these raters rate it and it is large enough. Reporting the reliability of the scores actually used, and what each index refers to (recommendation 1), is an instance of the transparency in creativity assessment that @barbot2019 call for. [\[FILL IN: verify the transparency standard attributed to barbot2019 (FI-17)\]]{.mark}

## Limitations and future research

First, the rating design was incomplete, and the analysis assumes that the missing ratings are ignorable given the allocation of products to raters. Actions were allocated to raters at random, which is in line with this assumption as far as it concerns which actions a rater rated, but random allocation of actions does not by itself make the number of ratings per product random. [\[FILL IN: the remaining details of the allocation in both rater pools (FI-4, FI-31)\]]{.mark} Ratings marked "action not recognised" were removed; if non-recognition depended on the action or the rater, the missingness is not ignorable. [\[FILL IN: non-recognition rate by rater (FI-22)\]]{.mark} The reliabilities by number of ratings are therefore observational.

Second, the two simulations rest on the assumptions stated in the Method: raters were drawn with equal probability, so that the raters' actual workloads are not reproduced; the parameters were treated as known, so that the ranges omit parameter uncertainty; and all ratings were generated from the fitted GRM with $\theta \sim N(0, 1)$, for one to 10 ratings and without selected or workload-weighted rater sets. The number of ratings needed is therefore a figure for this rater pool under these assumptions, and it presupposes the model and the latent distribution.

Third, the fit of the scoring model is not established. Local dependence was flagged for 36 rater pairs, with R02 in five of the 10 pairs listed, by a criterion that has no reference distribution and on a statistic that is negatively biased; the other checks had little power, because S-X² is conservative when most cells are imputed, C2 could not be computed, and infit and outfit values below 0.7 are expected with about two ratings per product. All reliability figures derived from the GRM (the empirical reliability of the obtained scores, rel~post~ and both simulations) rest on its posterior standard deviations and thus on local independence and on a normal latent distribution, although the ratings concentrated in the low categories; if these assumptions do not hold, the direction of any bias in these figures is unknown. Of the reliability and agreement figures, only Krippendorff's alpha and Cronbach's alpha do not depend on the model; the same holds for the raw response styles. The GRM is not a validated reference.

Fourth, the model comparison is not clear-cut: BIC disagreed with the LR tests and AIC on both constraints, as its heavier penalty per parameter allows, and the M1–M2 test is approximate for the reasons given under Model comparison in the Method.

Fifth, some rater parameters are imprecise, among them the thresholds of R18 and the discriminations of R26, R27 and R30; three of these four raters had about 50 ratings, but R26 had 136. The parameter-draw intervals are conditional on valid draws. The response styles have no uncertainty, no confidence intervals exist for the agreement statistics, and the thresholds of R27 are not comparable with those of the other raters.

Sixth, the raters came from two pools. [\[FILL IN: characteristics of both rater pools (FI-1, FI-21, FI-31)\]]{.mark} [\[FILL IN: whether the raters were selected for football expertise, or a statement that no such criterion was applied (FI-21)\]]{.mark} Whether they meet the CAT's requirement of domain familiarity was not established, and expertise was not analysed [@kaufman2009; @kaufman2013; @ceh2022; @hickey2001]. Together with the definition shown to the raters and the sparse design, this is one of the three departures from the CAT named in the Overview of the Method. Seventh, the exclusion of raters with fewer than 15 ratings was a technical estimation criterion; the refit with the excluded raters left the product scores virtually unchanged (see Model adequacy in the Results).

Eighth, the models had two facets and one dimension. They contain no facet for time or session, although rater tendencies can drift [@barth2021; @terai2026; @leckie2011; @myford2009] and workload affects agreement [@forthmann2017], and they do not test differential rater functioning [@wind2019a]; models such as the hierarchical rater model [@patz2002] or generalized many-facet models [@uto2020] could address this.

Several analyses were beyond the scope of this descriptive study and are left to future work: a held-out predictive check of model-based against raw-mean scores, a like-for-like comparison of the raw mean with every model, projections that include parameter uncertainty and use selected or workload-weighted rater sets, a prospective design with a calibration set rated by all raters, and rater covariates such as football expertise, including panels of licensed coaches.

# Conclusion

In these data, the empirical reliability of the creativity scores obtained for football actions (.695) was far below the pairwise Cronbach's alpha of .959, an approximate value that rests on 18 raters, and the model-based full-panel reliability of .970, a gap that belongs to the design and not to the raters. One or two ratings per action gave limited precision (.526 and .703), and in this rater pool the smallest number of ratings at which simulated reliability reached .80 was four. Raters differed in severity, scale use, discrimination and information. The shared category structure and equal discrimination were rejected by the LR tests and AIC but not by BIC; the scores of the four models ordered actions very similarly (Spearman's $\rho$ of .980 to .997 with the GRM scores) and, in an indicative comparison, more similarly than the raw mean and the GRM scores did. For nonverbal, time-pressured products such as football actions, rating-design figures from verbal or static material cannot be assumed to hold; they have to be collected for the product class and rater pool at hand. Studies of such products should report the reliability of the scores they use, plan several ratings per action, link raters through a common calibration set, and consider scoring with a model that adjusts for rater differences, reporting how far it departs from raw means. Whether such scores are more accurate remains to be examined.

The definition shown to the raters and the following objects are referenced in the main text.

## Definition of creativity shown to the raters {.unnumbered}

The raters read the following definition, in German or English, before the familiarisation clips, and it remained available at any time during rating (see Rating procedure in the Method). The English version is reproduced verbatim.

> Creativity is defined as the product of originality and functionality. A creative solution must be original (novel, rare, unusual) as well as functional (it must provide a solution to the given problem). Creativity in soccer describes the ability to choose solutions or execute actions in a given game situation that deviate from the norm, appear surprising, and are potentially advantageous for one's own team. It arises from the conscious perception of the situation and the recognition of possibilities that others do not see, or see only later. A creative action must be functional: it must (potentially) bring one's own team closer to the game objective (scoring, preventing goals). What matters is the intention or idea and the expected probability of success, not the actual outcome.
